questions.prompt: What is quantum entanglement?
questions.answer: Quantum entanglement occurs when the state of a composite system cannot be written as a product of separate states for its parts.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a product state and an entangled state?
questions.answer: A product state can be written as \(\lvert\psi\rangle_A\lvert\phi\rangle_B\). An entangled state cannot be factored into separate states for systems \(A\) and \(B\).

questions.prompt: Is the state \((\lvert 01\rangle+\lvert 10\rangle)/\sqrt2\) entangled?
questions.answer: Yes. The state is a Bell-type entangled state because it cannot be factored into a product of a state for the first system and a state for the second system.

questions.prompt: For \(\lvert\psi\rangle=(\lvert 01\rangle+\lvert 10\rangle)/\sqrt2\), what is the probability of measuring \(01\)?
questions.answer:
The amplitude of \(\lvert 01\rangle\) is \(1/\sqrt2\), so
\[
P(01)=\left|\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right|^2=\frac12
\]

questions.prompt: For \((\lvert 01\rangle+\lvert 10\rangle)/\sqrt2\), if the first system is measured as \(0\), what is the second system measured as?
questions.answer: It is measured as \(1\). In this state, the allowed outcomes are \(01\) and \(10\), so measuring the first system as \(0\) fixes the second as \(1\).

questions.prompt: For \((\lvert 01\rangle+\lvert 10\rangle)/\sqrt2\), what is the probability of measuring the first system as \(0\)?
questions.answer:
Only the \(\lvert 01\rangle\) term has the first system in state \(0\), so
\[
P(A=0)=\frac12
\]

questions.prompt: Does entanglement allow faster-than-light communication?
questions.answer: No. Entanglement creates strong correlations between measurement outcomes, but a local measurement result is still random and cannot be controlled to send a message faster than light.

questions.prompt: What do Bell tests show about entangled systems?
questions.answer: Bell tests show that quantum correlations can violate inequalities satisfied by local hidden-variable theories, ruling out that class of classical explanations.

questions.prompt: Write a common spin singlet state for two spin-one-half particles.
questions.answer:
\[
\lvert\psi\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\left(\lvert\uparrow\downarrow\rangle-\lvert\downarrow\uparrow\rangle\right)
\]

questions.prompt: For the spin singlet state, what happens if both spins are measured along the same axis?
questions.answer: The results are perfectly anti-correlated. If one particle is measured spin-up along that axis, the other is measured spin-down along the same axis.

questions.prompt: Show that \((\lvert 00\rangle+\lvert 11\rangle)/\sqrt2\) is normalized.
questions.answer:
The probabilities add to one:
\[
\left|\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right|^2+\left|\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right|^2=\frac12+\frac12=1
\]

questions.prompt: For \(\lvert\psi\rangle=(\sqrt3/2)\lvert00\rangle+(1/2)\lvert11\rangle\), find the probabilities of \(00\) and \(11\).
questions.answer:
\[
P(00)=\left|\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right|^2=\frac34
\]
\[
P(11)=\left|\frac12\right|^2=\frac14
\]

questions.prompt: Is \(\lvert0\rangle_A\lvert1\rangle_B\) entangled?
questions.answer: No. It is already written as a product of a state for system \(A\) and a state for system \(B\).

questions.prompt: Can two systems be correlated without being entangled?
questions.answer: Yes. Classical mixtures can have correlations without being in a single non-factorable quantum state. Entanglement is a specifically quantum kind of correlation in the state itself.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a Bell inequality?
questions.answer: A Bell inequality gives a bound on correlations expected from local hidden-variable theories. Entangled quantum systems can violate that bound.

questions.prompt: How does entanglement change the description of a two-particle system?
questions.answer: The pair must be described by one joint state. Assigning independent definite states to each particle misses the correlations contained in the combined wave function.

questions.prompt: For \((\lvert 00\rangle+\lvert 11\rangle)/\sqrt2\), what is the post-measurement state if the first system is measured as \(1\)?
questions.answer:
The joint state collapses to the compatible term:
\[
\lvert11\rangle
\]
so the second system is also \(1\).

questions.prompt: Why can a relative phase matter in an entangled state?
questions.answer: A relative phase changes interference between alternatives when the state is measured in other bases. States such as \((\lvert00\rangle+\lvert11\rangle)/\sqrt2\) and \((\lvert00\rangle-\lvert11\rangle)/\sqrt2\) can give different correlations in rotated bases.

questions.prompt: Show that \((\lvert00\rangle+\lvert01\rangle)/\sqrt2\) is not entangled.
questions.answer:
Factor out the first system:
\[
\frac{\lvert00\rangle+\lvert01\rangle}{\sqrt2}=\lvert0\rangle\frac{\lvert0\rangle+\lvert1\rangle}{\sqrt2}
\]
Because it factors into separate states, it is a product state.

questions.prompt: Why can \((\lvert00\rangle+\lvert11\rangle)/\sqrt2\) not be factored into separate one-system states?
questions.answer: A general product \((a\lvert0\rangle+b\lvert1\rangle)(c\lvert0\rangle+d\lvert1\rangle)\) contains amplitudes for \(00\), \(01\), \(10\), and \(11\). To remove \(01\) and \(10\), one needs \(ad=0\) and \(bc=0\), but keeping both \(ac\neq0\) and \(bd\neq0\) is then impossible. So the Bell state is entangled.
